p1.key: Addition polymerization joins monomers without losing any atoms, so the polymer has the same empirical formula and the same percentage of carbon as the monomer. The polymer has no C=C bonds and is less reactive.
CH<sub>3</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub> is propene. Its C=C double bond lets it undergo addition polymerization to poly(propene). The other compounds have no C=C bond outside an aromatic ring.
Covalent character decreases with electronegativity difference. Cs (0.8) and F (4.0) have the largest difference, so CsF is the most ionic / least covalent. SiO<sub>2</sub> is the most covalent.
A carboxylic acid (–COOH) and an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) condense, losing water, to form an amide link –CONH–. Esters form from acids + alcohols.
Each –COOH and –NH<sub>2</sub> join to form an amide link with loss of H<sub>2</sub>O, so nylon forms by condensation polymerization.

Amino acids condense, the –COOH of one with the –NH<sub>2</sub> of the other, forming an amide (peptide) link and water. Either acid can provide the COOH, so two different dipeptides (Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly) can form.
p1.flag: Amino acids/peptides are option (biochemistry) content; condensation link fits S2.4.

p1.key: Addition polymers form from monomers with a C=C double bond. Only but-2-ene is unsaturated; alanine forms condensation polymers, and butane and 1,2-dichlorobutane are saturated.
A polyamide contains repeating amide links –NH–CO– formed by condensation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid: B is nylon-6,6. A and C are addition polymers, and D is a polyester (–O–CO–). B.
A polyester forms by condensation polymerization of a diol with a dicarboxylic acid: each ester link releases H2O. These monomers have no C=C, so they cannot undergo addition polymerization.
The diamine and dicarboxylic acid join by amide links with loss of water. The repeat unit combines one of each: –HNCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH–COCH<sub>2</sub>CO–, i.e. option B.
The repeat unit is –CH<sub>2</sub>–CHCl–, so the monomer is chloroethene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl (A). C has no C=C and cannot undergo addition polymerization.

Nylon-6,6 forms from hexanedioic acid and H<sub>2</sub>N(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> with loss of water (condensation polymerization), and it contains –CONH– amide links, so it is a polyamide. All three statements are correct.

A condensation polymer needs a monomer with two functional groups. Ethane-1,2-diol forms a polyester and hexane-1,6-diamine forms a polyamide with the diacid. Ethylamine has only one NH<sub>2</sub>, so it can only end a chain.
The repeating unit is –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–: two main-chain carbons with one methyl group. That comes from propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>3</sub>.

An amine and a carboxylic acid condense, losing H<sub>2</sub>O, to form a secondary amide: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (written as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>). This is the same link that forms in polyamides. D is an ester and C is the salt.

A polyester needs two monomers that each have two functional groups: a dicarboxylic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) and a diol (ethane-1,2-diol). Ethanol (A, C) has only one OH, so it ends the chain. An aldehyde group (C, D) cannot form an ester link.

Propene CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>3</sub> opens its double bond to give the repeat unit –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–: one carbon carries two H, the other one H and one CH<sub>3</sub>. A is poly(ethene); B and C have the wrong substitution.

The repeat unit –OC–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–COO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O– is a polyester. It needs a dicarboxylic acid, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub>, and a diol, HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH; both monomers must have two functional groups to form a chain.

Condensation polymers need two functional groups on each monomer. II (diamine + dicarboxylic acid → polyamide) and III (two amino acids → polypeptide) qualify. In I ethanol has only one –OH group, so the chain cannot grow.
The repeating unit –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)– comes from opening the C=C of but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. But-1-ene would give a repeating unit with an ethyl side group.
Each repeating unit –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)– has a methyl group on both carbons, so the monomer is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Propene would give a methyl on alternate carbons only.

Addition polymerization needs a C=C double bond outside an aromatic ring. Ethylbenzene has only a benzene ring and a saturated side chain, so it cannot polymerize this way. Styrene (D), ethene (B) and the tetramethyl alkene (A) all have a C=C.
The repeating unit is –CH(Cl)–CH(CH3)–, so the monomer has these two carbons joined by a double bond: CHCl=CHCH3 (1-chloropropene).
Propene CH2=CH(CH3) opens its double bond, giving the repeating unit –CH2–CH(CH3)–. The CH3 stays as a side group.
